qr1:6ca17ea8cf71b681.title: Cancelling during post-download size/checksum verification is ignored: the file is published and the call resolves as success
qr1:6ca17ea8cf71b681.evidence: The function checks `signal?.aborted` only at entry (registry-download-utils.ts:105). The signal is also passed to the registry client for the transfer (lines 126-143). After the transfer it runs `fsPromises.stat`, then `measureChecksum(partialPath, hooks)` (line 155), which is a full SHA-256 stream over the file (utils/checksum.ts:8-31) and takes no signal. Then it calls `publishDownload(modelPath)` (line 165) and sends a 100% progress event, without checking the signal again. Callers handle cancellation only when this function throws `DownloadCancelledError`: registry.ts:566-578 deletes `.part` on cancel+clearCache, and registry-companion-set.ts:164-170 removes the set directory. A cancel that arrives during hashing is therefore never seen. registry.ts:581 returns `modelPath` as a successful load, and the clear-cache cleanup never runs.
qr1:6ca17ea8cf71b681.impact: The user cancels a model load (optionally with clear-cache) while a multi-GB GGUF is being hashed, which can take tens of seconds. The cancel has no effect: the SDK keeps hashing, publishes the file into the cache, reports 100%, and the load continues. A cancel with clear-cache leaves the full model on disk. For sharded or companion-set downloads, the loop moves on to the next shard, and that shard's transfer only then sees the aborted signal, so earlier shards stay published.
qr1:6ca17ea8cf71b681.reproduction: Unit test: stub `acquireRegistryClient` so `downloadBlob` writes a file of `expectedSize` to the `.part` path and resolves. Stub `measureChecksum` (or use a large file) to wait on a promise and call `controller.abort()` before resolving it with the right digest. Call `downloadSingleFileFromRegistry(..., controller.signal, ...)`. Observed: the call resolves, `modelPath` exists and a 100% progress event is emitted. Expected: it rejects with `DownloadCancelledError` and nothing is published.
qr1:6ca17ea8cf71b681.fix: Check the signal after the transfer and again right before publishing, for example `if (signal?.aborted) throw new DownloadCancelledError()` after `measureChecksum` and before `publishDownload`. Leave `.part` for the caller's clear-cache cleanup. Optionally, pass the signal into the checksum stream so it stops early.

verdict.reasoning: The headline claim, that the call resolves as success and the load continues, is false. It is true that downloadSingleFileFromRegistry (registry-download-utils.ts:105-176) checks the signal only at entry and in the registry client. measureChecksum (utils/checksum.ts:91) takes no signal. But callers never see the inner task's return value directly. downloadModelFromRegistry wraps the work in startOrJoinDownload (registry.ts:325, binding hooks?.requestBinding at :584). The public handlers pass that binding (handler.ts:101, download-asset.ts:48). In download-manager.ts:185-197, attachRequestBinding adds an abort listener. When the user cancels, that listener immediately settles the subscriber with InferenceCancelledError and removes it. Removing the last subscriber aborts the transfer controller (maybeCancelTransfer, :173). The user's load therefore rejects at once. When the background task later returns modelPath (registry.ts:581), downloadPromise.then (:276-281) loops over transfer.subscribers, which is now empty, so nobody receives a success. The 100% progress event goes to no subscribers for the same reason. The shard part is also wrong. After a shard publishes, the loop checks signal.aborted at registry.ts:199 and throws DownloadCancelledError. The catch at :395-408 then removes the whole shard dir when clearCache is set, so earlier shards do not stay published. Companion sets work the same way, per the claim's own note about registry-companion-set.ts:164-170. What remains is minor. On the plain single-file path, a cancel that lands during hashing does not stop the hash (wasted CPU/IO). The fully verified file is still renamed into the cache, so cancel with clearCache=true leaves a valid complete model on disk instead of deleting the .part file. That is a cache-hygiene and wasted-work issue, not a correctness or concurrency failure. The file is complete and checksum-verified, and no caller is misled.

qr1:50b76899eba2d613.title: Live spec fetch fails outright when the cache directory isn't writable, even though the download succeeded
qr1:50b76899eba2d613.evidence: fetchSpecLive calls mkdirSync(cacheDir) at parse-spec.ts:129 before fetching, and calls writeFileAtomically at :168-:172 after parsing. Neither call is wrapped. The cache is only an optimisation for the ETag and --offline paths, but any EACCES/EROFS/ENOSPC from these calls rejects parseSpecWithDependencies, so build-report.ts:100 never gets the entries it needed. The default CACHE_DIR is join(homedir(), '.cache', 'qvac') (:18).
qr1:50b76899eba2d613.impact: `qvac openai coverage` without --offline crashes with EACCES/EROFS in sandboxed CI, read-only HOME containers, or non-root Docker images with HOME=/. The spec was downloadable and parseable, and the cache isn't needed for a live run.
qr1:50b76899eba2d613.reproduction: Call parseSpecWithDependencies({}, { cacheDir: '/proc/qvac-cache', fetch: () => Promise.resolve(new Response(fixtureYaml, { status: 200 })), timeoutMs: 100 }). It rejects with an mkdir error instead of returning entries with sourceMode 'live'.
qr1:50b76899eba2d613.fix: Make cache I/O best-effort in live mode: wrap the mkdirSync and the three writeFileAtomically/rmSync calls in try/catch (optionally logging a warning) and still return { yaml, entries, source, sourceMode: 'live' }.

verdict.reasoning:
I read the code and the claim is correct. The live path is reached from a public command: `qvac openai coverage` without `--offline` goes from openai/command.ts to runOpenAiCoverage (coverage.ts:16), then buildCoverageReport (build-report.ts:100), then parseSpec, then fetchSpecLive.

In fetchSpecLive (parse-spec.ts:123-177), the call `mkdirSync(dependencies.cacheDir, { recursive: true })` at :129 runs before the fetch and is not wrapped in try/catch. The etag read at :132-137 is guarded, but this mkdir is not. After a successful 200 and a successful parseSpecYaml at :167, the code calls writeFileAtomically for the spec, sha256 and etag files (:168-172). Each of those calls mkdirSync, mkdtempSync, writeFileSync and renameSync (:110-121), and none of them is guarded. If any of them throws EACCES, EROFS or ENOSPC, the whole promise rejects and the entries that were already parsed are thrown away. The 304 fallback path (:144-158) also hits the same unguarded writes after its refetch.

Nothing upstream catches this. buildCoverageReport awaits parseSpec directly, and runOpenAiCoverage awaits buildCoverageReport directly.

There is no way around it from the CLI. CACHE_DIR is hardcoded to `join(homedir(), '.cache', 'qvac')` (:18), with no XDG_CACHE_HOME or environment override. The command offers only `--offline`, and that needs a cache which is already populated, so it doesn't help. buildCoverageReport does accept `specPath`, but the CLI never sets it: coverage.ts passes only `offline`.

None of the tests in openai-spec-fetch.test.ts cover an unwritable cache directory. Every test uses a writable mkdtemp directory, and nothing suggests the hard failure is intentional.

The impact is real but narrow. It needs a read-only or unwritable HOME, for example a container running with HOME=/ as non-root, a read-only rootfs, or a full disk. It affects one diagnostic or developer-facing command, it fails loudly instead of corrupting anything, and it doesn't touch the main runtime. Severity stays low.

qr1:0f8b4dce91d5fe48.title: Spec, SHA and ETag cache files are updated separately, so an interrupted or concurrent run leaves a hash-mismatched cache
qr1:0f8b4dce91d5fe48.evidence: parse-spec.ts:168-175 renames openai-spec.yaml, then openai-spec.sha256, then openai-spec.etag, each in its own atomic step. Each file is atomic on its own, but the set is not. If the process dies or the write throws (e.g. ENOSPC) between :168 and :169, the new spec sits next to the old SHA. If two CLI runs overlap across an upstream spec change, the writes can interleave (A.spec, B.spec, B.sha, A.sha). After that, validateCachedSpecHash (:56) throws 'cached OpenAI specification hash mismatch' for the --offline path (:200), and the ETag/304 path silently does a full re-download.
qr1:0f8b4dce91d5fe48.impact: After a Ctrl-C during the cache write, or two coverage runs at once (e.g. parallel CI jobs sharing HOME), `--offline` refuses a cache that holds a perfectly valid spec until someone runs online again.
qr1:0f8b4dce91d5fe48.reproduction: Stub writeFileSync so the second writeFileAtomically call throws, run parseSpecWithDependencies({}, deps-with-200), then run parseSpecWithDependencies({ offline: true }, deps). It rejects with 'hash mismatch' even though openai-spec.yaml holds the newly fetched, valid spec.
qr1:0f8b4dce91d5fe48.fix: Store spec, sha256 and etag together in one file (e.g. a JSON envelope or a header line), or write the SHA file first and the spec last so a partial update always fails toward a refetch. A per-cacheDir lock would cover concurrent runs.

verdict.reasoning:
The code matches the claim. In fetchSpecLive (parse-spec.ts:168-175) the spec, sha256 and etag files are written by three separate writeFileAtomically calls. Each call does a temp write and then renameSync (:110-121), so each file is replaced atomically, but nothing makes the three together atomic. There is no lock, no versioned directory and no combined manifest. The offline path (:197-213) reads the spec and calls validateCachedSpecHash(yaml, sha256Path, false). If the sha file exists but belongs to another spec, :56 throws 'cached OpenAI specification hash mismatch', which comes back as 'Offline mode requires a valid cached spec...'. The ETag path (:143-158) catches the same mismatch and silently fetches the whole spec again.

How reachable it is:
(1) Process death between :168 and :169. Lines 168-175 run synchronously, so a JS-level handler can't run in between. But Node installs no default SIGINT handler, so the OS can kill the process at any instruction. The window is microseconds, so this is possible but rare.
(2) An error between the writes, such as ENOSPC or EACCES on the second mkdtemp or write. This leaves the new spec next to the old sha. It is plausible but uncommon.
(3) Two processes sharing ~/.cache/qvac, for example parallel CI jobs. Their writes can interleave across processes. Only interleavings that span an upstream spec change produce a mismatch, so this is rare too.

Nothing else guards against it, and no comment says the behaviour is intended.

The impact is overstated in one way. The failure is loud and fixes itself: the error message tells the user to run without --offline once, and the online path fetches again and repairs the cache. No wrong data is used, since the hash check does its job. There is also a related variant the reviewer didn't mention: if the etag is newer than a matching spec+sha pair (writes interleaved as A.spec, A.sha, B.etag), a later 304 would serve spec A as 'not modified' even though the etag belongs to B. That is a silent stale-but-hash-valid result. The defect survives the checks, but given how narrow the windows are and how easy recovery is, severity stays low.

qr1:b777f3657c0c0f0d.evidence: deviceConfigDefaultsSchema (config.ts:54-81) is a plain z.object, so Zod strips unknown keys. It lists canonical keys for only 13 of the 17 ModelType values and only 9 aliases. ModelType (model-types.ts:10-42) also defines 'onnx-tts', 'bci-whispercpp-transcription', 'audiogen-ggml' and 'ggml-classification', plus the aliases 'bci', 'audiogen' and 'classification'. But both config loaders (inference/src/config/config-utils.ts:8 and sdk/src/client/config-loader/config-utils.ts:8) run qvacConfigSchema.safeParse, which removes these keys before they reach configRegistry.deviceDefaults (state.ts:145). getDefaultsFromPattern (model-config-utils.ts:120-135) then finds nothing for them.

The pattern is never applied, so on the target device the model loads with its normal backend/device, which is the problem the override was written to avoid (e.g. GPU crashes on specific Android devices).
qr1:b777f3657c0c0f0d.reproduction: `qvacConfigSchema.parse({ deviceDefaults: [{ name: 'x', match: { platform: 'android' }, defaults: { audiogen: { device: 'cpu' }, 'ggml-classification': { backend: 'cpu' } } }] }).deviceDefaults[0].defaults` returns `{}`. resolveModelConfigWithContext('audiogen-ggml', {}, { platform: 'android' }, thatPatterns) reports appliedPatterns = [].
qr1:b777f3657c0c0f0d.fix: Add schema entries for ModelType.onnxTts, bciWhispercppTranscription, audiogenGgml and ggmlClassification, and for the 'bci', 'audiogen' and 'classification' aliases, using their partial config schemas. Alternatively, call .strict() on the object so an unsupported key fails validation instead of disappearing. Better still, derive the key list from ModelType/CANONICAL_TO_ALIAS so new model types cannot be missed again.

verdict.reasoning:
I read the code to try to disprove the claim. It holds for audiogen, classification and bci. It is overstated for onnx-tts.

How the keys get dropped:
- `deviceConfigDefaultsSchema` (`packages/inference/src/schemas/config.ts:54-81`) is a plain `z.object(...).partial()`. It has no `.passthrough()` or `.catchall()`, so Zod drops any key it does not list. It lists 13 canonical keys and 9 aliases.
- Missing canonical keys: `onnx-tts`, `bci-whispercpp-transcription`, `audiogen-ggml`, `ggml-classification`.
- Missing aliases: `bci`, `audiogen`, `classification`. All three exist in `ModelTypeAliases` (`model-types.ts:50-63`).

The path is reachable from a public entry point:
- The SDK config loaders read the user's `qvac.config.*` file in `resolve-config.node.ts:63/76/105` and `resolve-config.expo.ts:28`. Both call `validateConfig`, which runs `qvacConfigSchema.safeParse` and returns `result.data` (`sdk/src/client/config-loader/config-utils.ts:8-14`; same in `inference/src/config/config-utils.ts`).
- The stripped data goes to the worker (`handler-utils.ts:23`, `setConfig`) and is stored as `configRegistry.deviceDefaults` (`state.ts:145`).
- On `loadModel`, `dispatch.ts:137-151` calls `resolveModelConfig`, then `getDefaultsFromPattern` (`model-config-utils.ts:120-135`). It looks up the canonical key, then `CANONICAL_TO_ALIAS[type]`. For `audiogen-ggml` that is 'audiogen', for `ggml-classification` 'classification', for `bci-whispercpp-transcription` 'bci'. These keys were already stripped, so it finds nothing.

Nothing else guards it:
- No error or warning is raised. The only log is a debug line that fires when a pattern was applied, and here none is.
- `MODEL_CONFIG_SCHEMAS` does register `audioGenConfigSchema` (which has device fields) and `bciConfigSchema`, so these defaults would be meaningful if they arrived.
- The comment at `config.ts:50-53` explains only the NMT/TTS passthrough. Nothing says the other types are left out on purpose.
- Tests call `resolveModelConfigWithContext` directly with in-memory patterns (for example `audiogen-plugin-config.test.ts:270`, which passes no patterns). That skips the schema parse, so no test covers this.

Where the claim is overstated:
- For `onnx-tts`, `CANONICAL_TO_ALIAS` maps to 'tts', which the schema keeps. A `"tts"` entry therefore still reaches onnx-tts models; only the literal `"onnx-tts"` key is dropped.
- There is a per-load workaround: pass `device` in `loadModel`'s `modelConfig`.
- The affected types are newer or niche.

Severity: a documented feature is silently ignored for some model types, but there is a workaround and it does not corrupt data. I rate it low-medium and chose medium.

verdict.reasoning:
The JSDoc on the public `deviceDefaults` config field (config.ts:222-226) says user patterns are "checked before the built-in patterns" and "First matching pattern wins." The implementation does something else. In resolveModelConfigWithContext (model-config-utils.ts:151-174), findAllMatchingPatterns uses `patterns.filter`, so it returns every match. The function then spreads the built-in matches and after them the user matches into mergedDefaults with `mergedDefaults = { ...mergedDefaults, ...defaults }`. The code's own comments state that this is intended: line 62 says "Ordered general → specific (later patterns override earlier)" and lines 155-156 say "Later values override earlier (more specific wins)". The test names agree: "user patterns override builtin patterns". So the implementation is deliberate and the doc comment is the stale part.

The path is reachable from public input. state.ts:219 passes `getConfig().deviceDefaults` unchanged (not reversed) as userPatterns, from qvac.config. Nothing reorders the patterns or warns about overlap. The reviewer's scenario holds. The fix is to correct the JSDoc. The "checked before" half is also misleading, though user patterns do still override built-in ones in effect. I'm rating it low-medium; I put low because nothing crashes and the existing semantics are coherent and tested. The impact is still a silently wrong device setting for users who follow the docs.

qr1:c1adc37dcb2bd3d7.title: Blob-core swarm topics are joined on every download and retry but never left, so DHT discovery sessions pile up
qr1:c1adc37dcb2bd3d7.evidence: downloadModel (client.js:361), downloadBlob (:465) and _reconnectCore (:310) all call hyperswarm.join(core.discoveryKey). Nothing in the file ever calls hyperswarm.leave(), including _doReleaseDownload (:578-612), which closes the blob core. In hyperswarm 4.17.x, join() (index.js:510-525) adds a PeerDiscovery to this._discovery and returns a new discovery.session(). Only leave() (index.js:529) destroys it. So every downloaded blob topic keeps being announced, looked up and refreshed on the DHT for the life of the client. Each retry adds one more session. hyperswarm.flush() (index.js:571-573) waits on `[...this._discovery.values()].map(v => v.flushed())`, so each new download's flush also waits on lookups for every topic joined before.
qr1:c1adc37dcb2bd3d7.impact: In a long-running SDK process that downloads many models, the client keeps doing DHT lookups and opening peer connections for blob cores it already closed. Memory and network use grow, and later downloads get slower to discover peers because flush() covers every stale topic.
qr1:c1adc37dcb2bd3d7.reproduction: Create a QVACRegistryClient and call downloadModel(..., {outputFile}) for N different models. After each one finishes, check client.hyperswarm._discovery.size: it grows to N+1 (the metadata topic plus N blob topics) and never shrinks. Peer connections keep being made for topics whose cores are closed.
qr1:c1adc37dcb2bd3d7.fix: Keep the discovery session returned by join(), or call this.hyperswarm.leave(core.discoveryKey) in _doReleaseDownload (ref-counted per discovery key so concurrent downloads of the same core don't drop each other's topic). Also avoid re-joining in _reconnectCore if the topic is already joined (for example, call discovery.refresh() on the existing session).

verdict.reasoning:
The literal fact holds: client.js:310, 361 and 465 call hyperswarm.join(core.discoveryKey, {client:true, server:false}) and nothing in client.js calls leave(). _doReleaseDownload (578-612) only closes blobs and core, and the swarm is torn down only in _close (837). But the claimed impact does not survive a read of hyperswarm 4.17.2:

1) Nothing is announced. Every join is client:true, server:false, so PeerDiscovery._refresh does dht.lookup, never announce (peer-discovery.js:108-118).

2) Discoveries do not pile up per download. Swarm.join (index.js:512-516) reuses the existing PeerDiscovery for a topic and only adds a lightweight PeerDiscoverySession. session.refresh() goes through discovery.refresh(), which returns the in-flight _currentRefresh when the mode is unchanged (peer-discovery.js:167-169). Repeated downloads and retries on the same blob core therefore add no extra DHT lookups. The only growth is a small object pushed to _sessions per call.

3) The number of distinct topics is bounded by the number of blob cores, not by downloads. On the server, blob cores come from _getOrCreateBlobsCore(label) (registry-service.js:1165-1179). That uses the activeBlobCoreLabel or BLOB_CORE_NAME, so there is one core per writer or rotation label. Many models share one core, each at its own blockOffset. A client downloading many models joins only a handful of topics.

4) flush() does not wait on old lookups. PeerDiscovery.flushed() awaits only _currentRefresh (peer-discovery.js:191-200), which is null between refreshes. Refreshes run every 10 min ±2 min (REFRESH_INTERVAL). A stale topic delays a flush only if a refresh happens to be running at that moment, and it does the same for the registry view topic, which is meant to stay joined.

What remains is a hygiene issue: a few blob-core topics keep a lookup every ~10 minutes after their core is closed. Keeping them joined arguably also speeds up the next resume or download from the same core. That is far from the claimed "memory and network use grow, and later downloads get slower". The impact is overstated, and the "sessions pile up / DHT announce" mechanism is wrong. Re-rated to low.

qr1:7788c40f8eb4a180.title: The abort listener added in _streamBlobToFile is never removed, so listeners and stream references build up on the caller's signal
qr1:7788c40f8eb4a180.evidence: Each call to _streamBlobToFile adds an 'abort' listener with { once: true } (client.js:760-768). The finally block (:771-778) destroys the streams and turns off the 'download' handler, but it never calls removeEventListener. A once listener is only removed when abort actually fires, so after a successful or failed attempt the closure (which holds stream, writeStream and reject) stays attached to the signal. withRetry calls _streamBlobToFile up to maxRetries times per download (:379-391, :489-499), and each attempt adds another listener.
qr1:7788c40f8eb4a180.impact: When a caller reuses one AbortSignal across many downloads (for example a session-wide cancel signal), listeners and the destroyed read/write streams they reference build up without limit. On Node this can raise MaxListenersExceeded warnings. A later abort then runs destroy/reject on stale streams from downloads that already finished.
qr1:7788c40f8eb4a180.reproduction: Create a single AbortController and run 20 downloadModel(path, source, { outputFile, signal: ctrl.signal }) calls one after another. On Node, use events.getEventListeners(ctrl.signal, 'abort').length: it reports 20 or more after every download has finished.
qr1:7788c40f8eb4a180.fix: Keep the handler in a variable, and in the finally block call options.signal.removeEventListener('abort', onAbort).

verdict.reasoning: client.js:753-769 adds an anonymous 'abort' listener with { once: true } to options.signal, and nothing ever removes it. The finally block (:771-778) destroys both streams, awaits the writer closing, destroys rangeDownload and turns off the core 'download' handler, but it never calls removeEventListener, and no AbortController is kept to remove the listener later. options.signal is the caller's signal passed straight through. The public download paths call _streamBlobToFile inside withRetry (:380, :490), so each attempt adds one more listener. Nothing wraps or derives the signal per download (a grep for AbortController in the file finds none). The path is reachable and nothing guards it: a caller that reuses one signal across downloads keeps one closure per attempt, holding stream, writeStream and reject. On Node, an AbortSignal with more than 10 listeners triggers the MaxListenersExceededWarning. The impact is overstated in one way. On a later abort, the stale listeners call destroy() on streams that are already destroyed, which does nothing, and reject() on promises that already settled, which also does nothing. So there is no wrong behaviour, only memory held until the signal is collected, plus the warning. This only happens when a long-lived signal is reused; with one signal per download it is garbage-collected together with the listeners. Severity stays low.

qr1:adf230d5a53d9f32.title: broker.pid records the CLI's own PID, so shutdown on Windows force-kills the CLI before its own cleanup runs
qr1:adf230d5a53d9f32.evidence: local-broker.ts:178 writes `process.pid` (the CLI process that hosts the embedded broker) into `<reportDir>/broker.pid`. The only consumer of `*.pid` files is `killTracked(reportDir)` (process-manager.ts:90-116), which reads every `.pid` file in reportDir and kills that PID. On win32 it runs `taskkill /PID <pid> /F /T`. `setupCleanup` in run-local.ts:221-229 calls `killTracked(reportDir)` first, then `extraCleanup?.()`, `brokerHandle.cleanup()`, `printLogPaths(reportDir)` and `process.exit(exitCode)`. Because broker.pid holds the CLI's own PID, `taskkill /F /T` force-terminates the CLI (and its whole tree) from inside killTracked, so none of the later steps run. On POSIX the self-sent SIGTERM is only queued, and the `cleaningUp` guard plus the synchronous `process.exit` hide the problem. verdict.reasoning:
I could not disprove the mechanism. In run-consumer-external.ts:33-36 the runner is spawned with no `detached` and with stdio 'inherit', so it stays in the terminal's foreground process group. Ctrl+C therefore sends SIGINT straight to the runner, and line 43 (`process.on('SIGINT', () => child.kill('SIGINT'))`) then sends it a second one.

The runner listens only with `process.once('SIGINT', ...)` (run-consumer-external-inplace.ts:134; in mqtt mode also external-consumer.ts:103). The first SIGINT removes that listener. When the last SIGINT listener goes, Node closes its signal watcher and SIGINT goes back to the default action. The forwarded signal arrives after the parent's event loop has handled its own SIGINT, which is usually milliseconds later and not close enough to merge with the first. So it most likely kills the runner while `await consumer.forceShutdown()` / `await executor.stop()` (lines 119-133) are still running.

The child then exits by signal with code null, and the parent runs `process.exit(code || 0)` (line 47), so it exits 0. Nothing guards against this: there is no `detached`, no check that the signal was already received, and no persistent handler. The same pattern is copied in run-consumer-desktop.ts:47 and the desktop runner's `once`, which suggests copy-paste rather than a deliberate choice.

The impact is somewhat overstated. Grandchildren with inherited stdio (the bridge interpreter and the mqtt-mode client) are in the same process group, so they get the terminal's SIGINT directly, and orphaning is less likely than the claim says. What is really lost is the consumer's MQTT forceShutdown/cleanup, plus a misleading exit code 0. This only affects interactive Ctrl+C in a dev/test CLI, so the severity stays low. Two waiters can both read the dead pid. A removes the lock and re-creates it with 'wx', then B's rm deletes A's fresh lock and B's 'wx' open succeeds. Both return true and both reach the spawn branch (lines 230-256). The mtime fallback (lines 105-107) has the same problem. Nothing downstream stops a second runner. A resumed 5 GB download that only fetched the last 100 MB reports 5 GB. These numbers feed operation metrics and are misleading for bandwidth and benchmarking analysis.
qr1:73718bee0297c2cf.reproduction: Unit test: call downloadModelFromHttpWithStats with downloadModelFromHttp mocked to call hooks.markCacheMiss() and then progressCallback({downloaded: 900, total: 1000}) followed by ({downloaded: 1000, total: 1000}), which mimics a resume from offset 900. The result has stats.totalBytesDownloaded === 1000, but only 100 bytes were transferred. Real repro: load a sharded HF model with profiling on, delete one shard file from the cache, load again, and compare totalBytesDownloaded with that shard's size.
qr1:73718bee0297c2cf.fix: Record a baseline from the first progress event received after markCacheMiss (or have producers report a transferred-bytes field) and store maxBytesDownloaded - baseline. Better still, add a `transferred` counter to the progress/hook contract (e.g. hooks.addBytesTransferred(n) called per chunk) and sum it instead of inferring transfer from absolute progress counters.

verdict.reasoning: I checked each part of the claim against the code and none of it holds up as a false alarm. wrapProgressCallback (download-stats.ts:57-67) skips progress only when collector.cacheHit === true. Otherwise it records max(fileSetInfo.overallDownloaded ?? shardInfo.overallDownloaded ?? downloaded). Nothing records the bytes already on disk at the start, so nothing is subtracted. computeStats (102-108) then reports that value as totalBytesDownloaded and divides it by elapsed time to get downloadSpeedBps. I confirmed each source the reviewer named. (1) http.ts:229-230 sets downloadedBytes = startOffset, the size of the partial file already on disk. When the server answers 206, the counter is not reset (it resets only for a non-206 reply, lines 302-306). The data handler then emits downloaded: downloadedBytes, which includes the prefix (393-397). The 416 branch (283-289) is worse: no cache hook is called, so cacheHit stays undefined, and it emits downloaded: startOffset. That reports the whole file as downloaded in roughly zero time. (2) In the HTTP sharded path, cached shards get downloadedBytes = expectedSize (780-784), markCacheMiss is called when any shard is missing (793), and overallDownloaded adds up every shard (1010). (3) In Hyperdrive, markCacheMiss runs at hyperdrive.ts:585, then already-valid files add their size to overallDownloaded and report it in progress (618-638). registry.ts:216 and registry-companion-set.ts:122 do the same thing, so the problem is wider than the reviewer said. These paths are reachable through the public loadModel/download flow whenever a download resumes or some shards are already cached. No caller or wrapper corrects for it. The comment at line 58 says cache-hit bytes should not count as network transfer, which shows this behaviour is not intended. No test sets an expected value for totalBytesDownloaded. The impact is limited to profiling gauges (types.ts:86-87, operation-metrics.ts:60-61) and does not affect downloads or model loading, so low severity is right.

qr1:a13711e07c6ae648.title: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the runner twice; the second one kills it partway through its graceful shutdown
qr1:a13711e07c6ae648.evidence: The child is spawned with stdio 'inherit' and no `detached` (run-consumer-external.ts:33-36), so it stays in the parent's foreground process group. When a user presses Ctrl+C, the terminal sends SIGINT to every process in that group, so the runner gets it directly. The parent's handler at line 43 then forwards a second SIGINT. The runner (runners/run-consumer-external-inplace.ts:134) registers `process.once('SIGINT', () => void shutdown())`. The first SIGINT uses up that one-shot listener and starts the async shutdown: `consumer.forceShutdown()` then `executor.stop()`. With no listener left, the second SIGINT falls back to Node's default action and ends the runner at once. The same happens in mqtt mode, because runMqttClient (utils/external-consumer.ts:103) also uses `once`. The parent then sees exit with signal=SIGINT and calls `process.exit(1)` (line 47).
qr1:a13711e07c6ae648.impact: An interactive Ctrl+C on `run:local:<name>` interrupts the consumer's MQTT force-shutdown and executor.stop(). The producer may not get the consumer's shutdown or offline notice, the bridge interpreter process may be left running, and the command exits with code 1 instead of 0.
qr1:a13711e07c6ae648.reproduction: Run `qvac-test run:local:external --name=<bridge consumer> --runId=x` in a terminal and press Ctrl+C once. The 'Force shutdown' path doesn't finish (no clean MQTT disconnect, the executor isn't stopped) and `echo $?` prints 1. Running `kill -INT <parentPid>`, which reaches only the parent, shuts down cleanly with exit 0.
qr1:a13711e07c6ae648.fix: Don't re-forward a signal the child already got from the terminal. Either spawn the child with `detached: true` (its own process group) and keep forwarding, or forward only SIGTERM and let the terminal's SIGINT reach the child on its own. Also switch the runner's handlers to `process.on` with an idempotent shutdown, so a repeated signal can't fall through to the default action.

verdict.reasoning:
The mechanism holds. run-consumer-external.ts:33-36 spawns the runner with stdio 'inherit' and no `detached`, so it stays in the terminal's foreground process group and gets Ctrl+C's SIGINT directly. Line 43 then forwards a second SIGINT with child.kill. The runner (run-consumer-external-inplace.ts:134) registers only `process.once('SIGINT', ...)`. Once that listener fires, Node's removeListener hook closes the signal handle and the default action comes back. The forwarded SIGINT reaches the runner after the parent's own event loop has run, which normally lands while the async shutdown is still in progress (forceShutdown, then executor.stop). The runner then dies by the signal, cut off partway through. I found nothing that guards against this: no `detached`, no re-armed listener, no ignore-after-first logic. consumer-base.ts:131 does mention double Ctrl-C, but it only makes forceShutdown idempotent and does not protect the process. In mqtt mode, external-consumer.ts:103 uses `once` as well. The path is reachable both from `qvac-test run:consumer:external` run directly and from `run:local:<name>`: routeRunLocal sends that to runLocalExternal, which uses spawnTracked (process-manager.ts:61). spawnTracked is also not detached, so the whole tree shares one process group.

Some of the claimed impact is overstated:
(1) Under run:local:<name>, run-local's own handler (run-local.ts:232) immediately sends SIGTERM to the producer and the consumer parent and calls process.exit(0). So the command's exit code is 0, not 1, and the producer is being torn down anyway, which makes a missed offline notice mostly moot. Exit code 1 and the lost notice to a separately running producer apply only when run:consumer:external is used on its own.
(2) The bridge interpreter is in the same foreground process group, so it also gets the terminal's SIGINT. In the common case it does not linger unless it ignores SIGINT.

What remains is a real but cosmetic or robustness issue on an interactive abort: the graceful shutdown is cut short, and the exit code is 1 in standalone mode. The same pattern is copied in the desktop, electron and snap commands. I'm downgrading severity to low.
